Demand & supply

How likely you are to sell it

—
chance of selling your whole harvest at a fair price
    What this assumes
    • Starts from a neutral 72% and moves with the country's import dependence, self-sufficiency, how big your harvest is next to national production, and how perishable the crop is.
    • "Fair price" means close to the FAOSTAT farm-gate average; you can almost always sell at a low enough price.
    • National data (FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets) — local markets, buyers' contracts and transport distance aren't modelled.
    • The weights are our own judgement, not a fitted statistical model.

    Supermarket contract

    An estimate from your crop, volume and setup, and the chains trading near you. No public data on supermarket contracts exists, so treat it as a guide.

    Looking for supermarket chains within 30 km…
    —
    chance of landing a supermarket supply contract
      What this assumes
      • Volume used is a year's supply: one harvest for grain, as many cycles as fit in a year for vegetables.
      • Starts at 25% for fresh produce and 4% for grain and pulses, then adds for volume, certification, packing, year-round supply, organic and nearby chains.
      • Nearby chains = supermarket brands with stores mapped on OpenStreetMap within 30 km; mapping is incomplete in some countries.
      • Capped at 70% (20% for grain and pulses) because buyers also weigh price, track record and relationships we can't see.
      • No public data on supermarket supply contracts exists, so the weights are our own judgement.

      Sources: FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (production, imports, exports and uses, latest year per country) · World Bank Commodity Price Data ("Pink Sheet") for bulk oil and meal prices · FAOSTAT producer prices for raw crops · supermarket chains from OpenStreetMap. Flour prices are estimated from the grain price (bulk ×1.45, premium stone-ground ×4 the grain price) — edit them with real quotes. Equipment costs are typical small-scale figures.
